## Introduction

Git is a free, open-source, distributed version control system (VCS) designed
to track changes in source code during software development. It allows
developers to manage project history, collaborate with others, and work on code
simultaneously without overwriting each other's work.

Git was created By Linus Torvalds because he needed version control when
building the Linux kernel. And now, according to the 2022 Stack Overflow
developer survey, 96% of professional developers use Git.

Although, Git is not only a tool for developers, its a way of life. Almost any
texted based project could be maintained using Git. It is in your best interest
to track and save your work using Git, your homework, notes, writing and
personal projects. 

This workshop will take you through the process of creating and managing a
hypothetical project using Git. Along the way you will learn the commands
concepts and best practices required manage your own work using Git and GitHub.

## Setting up your repository

If you are on macOS or Linux, you should open your preferred terminal emulator.

If you are using Windows, then I suggest that you use Git Bash. Git Bash
provides Unix-like command line utility which is what this workshop was
designed for.

First, change directory into where ever you would like to keep your project
folder. 

For the purpose of consistency I will use the `~/Documents` folder.

```zsh
cd ~/Documents
```
> `cd` stands for "change directory" the argument we pass is the directory we
> would like to change into. We will use this command often.

::: {.callout-note}
Unix-like operating systems have a different directory structure than Windows.
Although, this command will work as expected if you are using Git Bash.
:::

Now, create a project directory:
	
```zsh
mkdir ./example_project
```
> `mkdir` stands for "make directory" the argument we pass is the name of the
> directory that we would like to create. The `./` means within our current
> directory.


Change directories into the new directory we just created.

```zsh
cd ./example_project
```

Then lets initialize a new Git repository:
	
```zsh
git init
```

Now lets list all of files within the current directory:

```zsh
ls -a
```
> `ls` stands for "list segments", it will list the contents of the current
> directory. The `-a` argument means "all", this allows us to see the hidden
> files. Hidden files start with `.`.

You will see that a new directory: `.git/`. This is what makes a directory a Git
repository. This `.git/` directory is where Git keeps track of everything it
needs to provide you will all of its functionality.

In all, `git init` is how we tell Git that we would like to track this specific
directory. Git tracks the directory using the `.git/` sub directory.

Once a directory is initialized and being tracked by Git it is considered a
**repository**.

## Configuration

You can configure Git to your desired behavior using `git config`. Git provides
many options by default in order to customize your experience. It is not
possible to remember every option that you may need in the future so you should
use the [git manual](https://git-scm.com/docs), the internet and AI to help you.

Git configuration is hierarchical and can be represented like this:

```{mermaid}
flowchart TD
    subgraph SYSTEM["System - All"]
        subgraph GLOBAL["Global - Current user"]
            subgraph LOCAL["Local - Current repo"]
                subgraph WORKTREE["Worktree"]
                end
            end
        end
    end

    style SYSTEM fill:#f9dcc4,stroke:#e07a5f,color:#000
    style GLOBAL fill:#d4e8c2,stroke:#3a7d44,color:#000
    style LOCAL fill:#c4d9f9,stroke:#3a5fa8,color:#000
    style WORKTREE fill:#e8c4f9,stroke:#7a3aa8,color:#000
```

The more specific a configuration, the higher its priority. For instance, a
local option will be applied over a global one if they have both set different
values for the same configuration. Although, most of the time you will just
configure global settings.

In addition, it is important to note that when configuring Git, we are just
changing a text file with key-value pairs of the desired option.

| Layer     | Scope                        | Location                                   |
|-----------|------------------------------|--------------------------------------------|
| System    | All users on the machine     | `/etc/gitconfig`                           |
| Global    | Your user account            | `~/.gitconfig`                             |
| Local     | Single repository            | `.git/config`                              |
| Worktree  | Single worktree in a repo    | `.git/worktrees/<worktree>/config.worktree`|

: This table shows the location of each configuration file.
	

Lets try an example:

First lets check to see if your username and email are set:

```zsh
git config --get user.name
git config --get user.email
```
> The `--get` argument does not change anything, it only prints the
> corresponding option.

If they are not set, then I recommend that you change them to your GitHub
username, and email. Since Git configuration is just a file, we could either
edit the file directly or use the commands that Git provides. It is standard
practice to use the command line for configuration since there is less chance
for a syntax error.

```zsh
git config --add --global user.name "github_username_here"
git config --add --global user.email "email@something.com"
```
> The `--add` argument means we will add the desired value to the configuration.

It is also good practice to set your default branch:

```zsh
git config --add --global init.defaultBranch main
```

We can look at the global configuration file using this command:

```zsh
cat ~/.gitconfig
```
> `cat` means "concatenate" it allows us to print the contents of a desired
> file passed as an argument.

Alternatively, you could see all active configuration values across all layers
at once:

```zsh
git config --list
```

Your terminal may print something like this:

```
[user]
        name = mikeagga
        email = mikeag916@gmail.com
[init]
        defaultBranch = master
        defaultBranch = main
```

We can interpret the structure of the Git configuration files. These files are
broken into sections which contain key value pairs. In the example above there
are two sections. These sections correspond to the command we ran earlier: `git
config --add --global init.defaultBranch main`. The first value `init` becomes
the section. The second value `defaultBranch` becomes key. Lastly, `main` will
be the value.

In addition, you may notice that there are two `defaultBranch` keys. This
happened because I used `git config --add` twice. In this case Git will use the
latest entry which is `main`. You should use `git config --set`, which will
override the configuration if said key-value pair already exists.

Although Git provides many configuration options that effect behavior, there is
nothing stopping you from setting whatever options that you would like
arbitrarily.

Lastly, you may come across many different commands and methods of configuring
Git. Although, a conceptual understanding of how the configuration files are
structured will make interpreting these commands and methods just a matter of
remembering procedure.

## Basics

The core functionality of Git is the ability to save your work, this is called a
commit. Git gives you the ability to control which files are committed and
when. Git will label any given file with one of three states. These states are
how we control what files are committed, and what files are not.


| State       | Description                                     |
|-------------|-------------------------------------------------|
| `untracked` | Git is not tracking this file at all.           |
| `modified`  | A tracked file that has changes not yet staged. |
| `staged`    | Marked for inclusion in the next commit.        |

Run this command in your repository:

```zsh
git status
```
This command allows us to check how Git has labeled each file in our repository.
Currently our repository is empty, so there is nothing to see.

Now lets make create a new file:

If you are familiar with a terminal based text editor like vim or nano I
encourage you to use it here. If not, you can load this current directory using
an IDE like VScode for example.

You should check your working directory with this command:

```zsh
pwd
```
> `pwd` means "print working directory" it will print the path of your current
> directory.

Within this directory create a new file called "hello.md".

Within the file write:

```
Hello world!
```
Save it, then head back into your terminal instance.

```zsh
git status
```
You will see that the new file "hello.md" that we just created is considered
untracked. We would like to keep track of "hello.md", so run:

```zsh
git add hello.md
```
> You can stage a file or entire sub directory. You can even stage the entire
> repository using `git add .`.

Now, check the status again:

```zsh
git status
```

You will see that "hello.md" is now a staged file. Meaning it will be included
in our next commit.

Finally, we can make a commit:

```zsh
git commit -m "Add hello.md"
```

The `git commit` command will save a snapshot of the staged files, the argument
`-m` means that the preceding text within the quotation marks will be the commit
message. Our commit message should be short and informative.

::: {.callout-note}
Git does not store entire files, nor does it track the difference between
changed files. It is more accurate to view a commit as a picture, or a
screenshot of your project directory at the time of your commit. 
:::

In general, this is the core functionality of Git. Create or edit a file, stage
it using `git add`, then commit it using `git commit`. These commands along with
`git status` and `git push` may account for around 90% of your Git usage.

It is a good idea to commit your work often especially when coding. You will be
able to track all of the changes that you have made, and look back at your
project in earlier stages. In addition, there is very little downside to having
many commits. According to the Git website: "As of 2025, the current version of
the Linux kernel's source code is 1.7 GB. Git stores the full history of the
Linux project (1.4 million commits) in only 5.5 GB.". Git is designed to be very
efficient with storage, and very powerful in utility. 


## Structure of a commit

Git keeps track of all of our commits and all of our files within our directory
at the time of the commit. Understanding a little about how Git keeps track of
everything will help demystify Git conceptually and will make understanding
later concepts a bit more simple.

We can view our commit history using this command:

```zsh
git log
```

This command is very useful for understanding the structure of your commits. We
will use it often. 

Currently, we only have a single commit. Which should look something like this:

```
commit b556efb1dcb4bdbfd971b615e8dae4cd26882f91 (HEAD -> main)
Author: mikeagga <mikeag916@gmail.com>
Date:   Sun Feb 15 16:14:11 2026 -0500

    Add hello.md
```

This string of seemingly random characters is a hash. This is a method of
condensing data in a way that is reproducible. Specifically, it's a SHA-1 hash
of the commit object's contents. This is called the **commit hash** and it
contains information about our commit.

We can inspect the contents of this commit hash using this command:

`git cat-file -p YOUR_COMMIT_HASH_HERE`

> You only need to provide the first 4 characters of the hash, so no need to
> type it all out.

```
tree 9155d858058637fd4552c960d7f11546e579850b
author mikeagga <mikeag916@gmail.com> 1771190051 -0500
committer mikeagga <mikeag916@gmail.com> 1771190051 -0500

Add hello.md
```

It appears that `git log` uses some information from the commit hash in order to
print what it needs.

In addition our commit hash contains another hash, this time it is a **tree
hash**. This hash contains information about the working directory or "working
tree" at the time of the commit.

We can also inspect this tree hash:

`git cat-file -p YOUR_TREE_HASH_HERE`

This is the result:

```
100644 blob a0423896973644771497bdc03eb99d5281615b51    hello.md
```

We have only committed one file therefore our working tree hash only stores one
file. This file is represented by another hash called a **blob**.

We can inspect the contents of this blob:

`git cat-file -p YOUR_BLOB_HASH_HERE`

This is the result:

```
hello world!
```
We can see that a blob is how Git stores the contents of our files.

In summary, Git uses three primary types of objects, each identified by a hash:

| Object | What it stores |
|---|---|
| Commit | Metadata (author, date, message) and a pointer to a tree. |
| Tree | A snapshot of your project directory, containing pointers to blobs. |
| Blob | The raw contents of a single file. |
: There are more object types but they are beyond the scope of this explanation.


```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
    Commit["Commit<br/>b556ef...<br/>Add hello.md"]
    Tree["Tree<br/>9155d8..."]
    Blob["Blob<br/>a04238...<br/>(hello.md)"]

    Commit --> Tree
    Tree --> Blob
```
> This is the structure that we have observed.

In order to demonstrate how Git efficiently tracks many files, lets make another
commit.

First, within your repository create a new file using your text editor or IDE.

Call this file: "contents.md"

Within this file write:

```
contents
```

Save the file. Then, back in your terminal:

Mark the file as staged:

```zsh
git add contents.md
```

Commit the file:

```zsh
git commit -m "Added contents"
```
Then, view the commit history:

```zsh
git --no-pager log --oneline --parents
```
> The additional arguments just make the result easier to interpret. 

The result:
```
f700dd5 b556efb (HEAD -> main) added contents
b556efb Add hello.md
```

Our second commit has two hashes next to it, the first hash is its own, the
second is its parent. Our original commit had no parents, since it was the
first.

Each subsequent commit will point to the last, this is what gives commits
structure.

We can investigate our new commit's hash:

```zsh
git cat-file -p YOUR_COMMIT_HASH_HERE
```

The result:
```
tree f9d01e625a573fa544c00a0d4acf98c985006c71
parent b556efb1dcb4bdbfd971b615e8dae4cd26882f91
author mikeagga <mikeag916@gmail.com> 1772047353 -0500
committer mikeagga <mikeag916@gmail.com> 1772047353 -0500

added contents
```

Notice that the tree hash is different then the tree hash of our first commit.

Lets investigate the contents of this new tree hash:

```zsh
git cat-file -p YOUR_TREE_HASH_HERE
```

The result:
```
100644 blob 12f00e90b6ef79117ce6e650416b8cf517099b78    contents.md
100644 blob a0423896973644771497bdc03eb99d5281615b51    hello.md
```
Now there are two blobs which represent both files at the time of our latest
commit. Notice that: since we never changed hello.md, the blob hash remains the
same thought the tree hash has changed.

We can represent this behavior with a graph:

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
    CommitA["Commit<br/>b556ef...<br/>Add hello.md"]
    CommitB["Commit<br/>f700dd...<br/>Added contents"]
    TreeA["Tree<br/>9155d8..."]
    TreeB["Tree<br/>f9d01e..."]
    BlobHello["Blob<br/>a04238...<br/>(hello.md)"]
    BlobContents["Blob<br/>12f00e...<br/>(contents.md)"]

    CommitB --> CommitA
    CommitA --> TreeA
    CommitB --> TreeB
    TreeA --> BlobHello
    TreeB --> BlobContents
    TreeB --> BlobHello
```

Each commit points to its own tree, which represents the state of your project
at that moment in time. Since "hello.md" was unchanged, both trees point to
the exact same blob. 

This use of structured hashing is what makes Git so efficient even with large
projects with long histories. Only the files that have changed take up new
space.

## Branching

Now that we understand some of the inner workings of Git, we can explore more of
its functionality. I previously mentioned that commits are structured so that
linearly so that subsequent commits point to earlier ones.

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
    A["Initial commit"]
    B["Second commit"]
    C["Main work"]

    A -->|main| B
    B -->|main| C
```
> Our primary branch is `main`. The arrows point to later commits. Each arrow is
> labeled with the branch for clarity.

One of the most useful features Git provides is **branching**. A branch is
simply a pointer to a commit, allowing you to diverge from your current line of
development while leaving it intact. This makes it possible to work on new
features, experiments, or fixes in isolation, without affecting the rest of the
project.

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
    A["Initial commit"]
    B["Second commit"]
    C["Main work"]
    D["Feature work"]

    A -->|main| B
    B -->|main| C
    B -->|feature| D
```
> This shows an example where a branch `feature` was created after the second
> commit, then commits were made to both `main` and `feature`.

We can list all of the branches in our repository with:

```zsh
git branch
```

Currently we only have our default branch: `main` which we set the name of
earlier.

Create a new branch:

```zsh
git branch test
```
> `test` is the name of the branch that we are creating.

We can then switch to a specified branch. 

```zsh
git switch test
```

Lets make a commit on this branch:

Create a new file "groceries.md", within the file add:

```
Eggs
Cheese
Milk
```

Save it, then back in the terminal: 

Stage "groceries.md":

```zsh
git add groceries.md
```

Then commit it:

```zsh
git commit -m "added grocery list"
```

We can again look at the commit history:

```zsh
git log
```

You can see that all of our previous commits to `main` are listed here, in
addition the commit that we have just made is also listed. 

Now switch back to `main`:

```zsh
git switch main
```

Now use the following in order to compare the commit history between branches:

```zsh
git log
```

You will see that the commit that we made to `test` is missing. 

This is the functionality of branches, our `test` branch will preserve the
history and changes up to the time the new branch is created. Any changes on one
branch will have no effect on other branches. This allows you to take a project
in a new direction, without effecting the original project.

Lets create another commit on `main`

Double check that you are still on the primary branch `git branch`

Create a new file: "movies.md"

Within the file add:

```
The God Father
The Dark Night
Back To The Future
```

Now, `add` and `commit` this file be sure that you are on `main` and use the
commit message "added movies.md".

Run the following:

```zsh
git log --oneline --graph --all --decorate --parents
```
> The argument `--decorate` will allow us to see the commit history across
> branches. The rest of the arguments for your convince. 

You could see that these most recent commits share the same parent. This is the
idea behind divergence and illustrates how branches represent a new commit
history at a chosen point.

## Merge


Imagine you are using Git to manage the creation of a Website. Imagine that you
have created a new branch to test some different colors for the background of
this website. Now lets say that you like how these changes look, and want the
main branch to incorporate the changes. There are a few ways to do this, one way
would be to merege the branches. 


There are a few basic types of merges that will be good to know about.

The first is a fast forward merge. This is when you create a commit on a new
branch, and there have been no new commits on the main branch. In this case, you
could imagine that Git treats this branch as now just part of main.

INSERT IMAGE OF FFMERGE

The second is a merge commit. This is where you would like to merge your feature
onto main, but there has been a commit on main. Git deals with this deviation
through creating a new commit which connects the deviated histories of both
branches.

INSERT IMAGE OF merge commit.

In our case, we have already moved forward with main, after creating a new
feature branch. Thereby we will be using a merege commit.

Lets merge our branches to demostrate what this may look like:

Double check that you are on the correct branch. When merging branches, you
should be sure that you are on the brach that you would like to incorperate the
changes onto. For us, that is `main`.

then use `git merge test`

where `test` is the branch to merge.

Now look at the commit history:
`git log --oneline --graph --all --decorate --parents`

You will see that now this merge commit has two parents, one from the `test`
branch and the other from `main`.

We know that git allows you to manage your projects history, one significant
part of managing a projects history is that you may have to revert to older
versions. Say for instance you commit a change that breaks the project. Git

It may be apparent that since a merege commit has two parents, reverting will
get complicated. Since the commit history is split between two branches, git
will give you a difficult time. This will cause many headaches if you happen to
need to revert to a point before a merge commtit. Therefore it is always best to
avoid merge commits and only use fast forward merge. It is best practice to
instead use `rebase` when working in a local repository.

## Rebase

First we will undo the merge commit that we just made:

`git reset --hard HEAD~1`

This is safe since we have not made any other commits, and we have not pushed it
to any remote repo.

We will learn what this command does in the next section.

If you look at the commit history with: 
`git log --oneline --graph --all --decorate --parents`

You will see that the merge commit is removed.

Rebasing is essentailly rewriting history. Rebasing takes the changes from a
feature branch then places them after the latest commit, making the history
linear and simple to navigate. 

First we need to switch branches to our feature branch:

`git switch test`

Then run:

`git rebase main`

Now check out the commit history: 

`git log --oneline --graph --all --decorate --parents`

You will see that all of the commits that were on our feature branch are now
just added to the end of our main branch. Our commit history is now simple and
linear making restetting very simple. Take note that rebasing simply moved where
our branch splits from our main branch. The branch still exists.

In preceding sections we will learn about working collabratively on a single
repository. It is important to know that you should never rebase onto a branch
that someone else is working on. This will cause the commit history of that
branch to be vastly different. In this case you should use `git merege`, I will
explain in detail later.

A good rule of thumb: When contributing to shared projects, use Rebase to keep
your local history clean and synchronized while you work. When you are ready to
integrate your work into the main codebase, use Merge to preserve the final
history of the feature.

We can now imagine that we are done working on this new feature branch that we
have created, meaning that we no longer need this branch. After rebasing, our
feature branch is located at the tip of our main branch. This means that we
could now safely fast forward merge this branch.

Be sure that you are on the main branch.

`git switch main`

then run: `git merge test` in order to merge our feature branch onto main.

if you then run:
`git log --oneline --graph --all --decorate --parents`

You will notice that no merge commit is created and `test` has now been merged
onto main.

if you then run `git branch`, you will see that our feature branch still exists.

Since we are done using this branch, we will remove it using:

`git branch -d test`

We have successfully implemented our feature branch onto our main branch so that
our commit history remains clean and cleaned up our repository to only contain
our main branch.


## Reset

We took a look at rebasing so that you have a more effective linear structrure
to your commit history. Since git gives us full control over how our commit
history is structured, walking back up our commit tree with a reset becomes very
powerful.

You will have noticed that when looking at our commit history using `git log`
that the latetest commit is always labled with `HEAD`. `HEAD` is what git uses
to mark whichever the latest commit on whichever branch that you are on.

There are three types of resets that git provides. The first that we will use is
a soft reset. A soft reset moves the `HEAD` pointer back to a specified point,
thus undoing the commits until that point, this type of reset does not alter
your working tree in any way, nor does it effect your staged files. So only the
commit history is effected.

Run:

`git reset --soft HEAD~1`

The last argument `HEAD~1` just means that we will reset 1 commit back from the
head pointer. In addition, you could also use the commit hash of a specific
commit instead of `HEAD~1`. Remember you could see the commit hash using `git
log`

Now look at the commit history.

`git log --oneline --graph --all --decorate --parents`

You will see that our previous commit gone.

Now run: `git status`

You will see that the contents of the previous commit are still tracked or
staged. 

We now have the opportunity to change the staged file, or add another file to
the commit. For now, just re-commit the files that are currently staged.

`git commit -m "new commit message"`

One use of `git reset --soft` is you would like to change the commit message of
the most recent commit. You should also use soft resets if you forgot to stage a
change that you would like to have in said commit. In addition, you could soft
reset multiple commtis if you would like to group all of the commits into one.

The next type of reset is a mixed reset. This reset is very similar to soft
reset, but does not re-stage the files. You can do it using: `git reset HEAD~1`

There is no need to try it now, just keep it in mind if you need to use it at
some point.

Lastly is hard reset. This will take your repository back to the time of the
specified commit. 

To illustate this, lets first take a look at our current repository with:

`ls`

Now, lets make another commit:

Make a new file called: "bad_mistake.md"

Within the file write:

"This is a super bad mistake that broke my project."

Then stage the file, and commit it with message: "mistake commit"

Also take note of the commit tree.

`git log --oneline --graph --all --decorate --parents`

Now, lets hard reset to a time where we didn't commit a project breaking file.

Run: `git reset --hard HEAD~1`

We can then use `ls` to see that `mistake.md` is no in the repository. We could
also take a look at the commit history once again.

`git log --oneline --graph --all --decorate --parents`

You will see that the mistake commit is gone entirely and our working tree is
reset to how it was after the previous commit.

This may be exactly what you would like to do, but say for instance you realized
that there was something important in the last commit that you just hard reset.
Luckily git has a way to help you out of this situation.

Git keeps track of ever time the head pointer moves, this is called the reflog.

We can use `git reflog` to view the changes to the head pointer that git has
tracked.

To reset to a time before we hard reset, we could take a look at the reflog and
find the commit before the reset and make note of the commit hash.

Then use: `git reset --hard HEAD@{1}` 

**Note that we could either use the commit hash or use pointer arithmatic,
just be sure that it is correct.**

We could now run `ls`, you will notice that `bad_mistake.md` is back in the
working tree.

And if you take a look at the log:

`git log --oneline --graph --all --decorate --parents`

You will see that "mistake commit" is back in the commit history!!

## Remote

I mentioned that a big component of modern git is working collaboratively, this
is typically done through Github. Although, to beginners Github is a bit of a
mystery. To demystify GitHub a bit, I will demonstrate the workflow for an
indivdual using a local remote repository.

Through the use of the `git remote` set of commands, git allows you to connect
your repo to other repos. Usually there is one main repository which all
collaborators consider the "source of truth" usually named "origin". This
repository is where the finalized code will stay. Typically, this will be the
repository that Github hosts for you.

Lets imagine that our current repository is the source of truth that we would
like to connect to.

First lets start by creating another repository: 

`cd ../`

Use this command to change directory into the previous directory. It is very
important that you do not make the new repository inside the example project
repository that we were just in.

`mkdir ./example_project_local/`

Make a new directory, this will simulate the local repository.

`git init`

Remember, we initalize a git repo using this command.

Now, connect our original repository using this command:

`git remote add origin ../example_project`

Where origin will be the name of the connected remote repository it could be
anythign but "origin" is the converntion. The last argument will be the source,
in this example it is the path to our original project repository. If Github is
the source, then this argument will be a url.

Use the following command list the connected remotes and verify that we have
connected our remote correctly. 

`git remote -v`

We can now run `git log`, you will see that there is currently no commit
history. 

now run `git fetch`.

This command will fetch the commit history. We can confirm this via running
`git log` once again.

You will notice, our simulated local repository does have the same commit
history, but does not contain any files. You will also notice that the commit
hashes are the same across both repositories.

Now use `git merge origin/main` to merge the contents 

Now you could use `ls`, you will see that all of the files from the other
repository are now copied into our current repository. In addition, we have
learned that you could pass remote branches to the `git merge` command.

We could also push file from our local directory into our source of truth
repository. Meaning, we could create edit and commit changes within our local
repository, then cause our upstream mirror repository (source of truth) to sync
to our local repository. This means our local objects, reference and commit
history will be synced to our upstream repo.

To reiterate, our source of truth is whatever repository we choose, most of the
time it will be a git repository hosted on GitHub, it is an arbitrary choice
that is standard practice. One thing to note is that a GitHub directory is a
"bare" repository, meaning that GitHub does not actually store all of your
files, and instead only keeps track of the `.git/` directory within your
repository. This makes the repository much different than our example source of
truth repository. For instance, there is no working tree in a bare repo,
therefore, no one is technically "checked-out", or "within" the repository. This
then means that you could freely push to a bare repo with no issues. On the
other hand, our upstream repo is not bare and we currently have main checked
out. If we push our changes from our local repo to main while main is checked
out then our HEAD pointer would be one commit behind, and we would cause issues
if we tried to make another commit.

ADD A PICTURE EXAMPLE

Lets demonstrate this with an example:

First, create the file: "example_push.md" within your `example_project_local/`
directory. 

With contents: 

```
This is an example of how to use the push command.
```
Then `add` and `commit` it with message: "Added example_push.md"

Now run: `git push origin main`, where origin is the name of the remote, and
main is the name of the branch.

You will see a scary looking error message. This error message is protecting us
from the problem that we discussed earlier, also the push was not successful.

***Note, if our upstream repository was bare, then this command would not throw
and errors***

This is the same issue that arises when working collaboratively within one
repository. Imagine you push your changes to main, while another collaborator is
has main checked out. This issue could be circumnavigated through branching,
which is the standard practice for contributing to a collaborative project.

Now run: `git reset --soft HEAD~1` a command that we learned earlier that will
undo the latest commit but preserve the working tree.

Then run: `git switch -c temp_branch` 

This command is shorthand to create a new branch and switch to it, the last
argument is the chosen name of the branch.

Then commit the changes to this new "temp_branch" with the same commit message.

Now run: `git push origin temp_branch` in order to push our changes upstream.

Then change directories back into our simulated upstream repo:
`cd ../example_project`

Now run `git branch` to check that the new branch as been created, then switch
into the new branch and use `ls` to check that "example_push.md" is there.
Finally, switch back to the main branch.

We can also take a look at the commit history: 
`git log --oneline --graph --all --decorate --parents`

You will notice that, since "temp_branch" starts at the tip of "main", we can
use a fast-forward merge.

Use: `git merge temp_branch` to perform a fast-forward merge.

Now it is a good practice to delete the branch after merge using:
`git branch -d temp_branch`.
